items.title: Life after removal, livestreamed
items.dek: Deported from the United States to countries they barely remember, some people have turned their phones into a record the state never bothered to keep. A piece in The Nation asks what viewers owe them.
paragraphs: A deportation, in the eyes of the state, ends at the airport. The removal is logged, the case closed, the person subtracted from the national ledger. What happens next, as the sociologist Sarah Tosh of Rutgers points out in a new piece for The Nation by Iliana Hagenah, is simply not counted: the United States records how many people it expels but keeps no overall account of how their lives unfold afterwards.

Into that silence a small genre has stepped. Hagenah profiles deportees who film their new lives for social media, producing everything from food clips and travel vlogs to something closer to citizen journalism. Laymone Khambounleung, who posts as Mones, grew up in Louisiana after his family fled Laos for Thai refugee camps when he was a baby; he never applied for citizenship, cycled through jail for nonviolent offences, and was sent back to Laos after Washington pressured the country in 2025 to take deportees. He now lives with relatives and says his aim is to show that people can change.

The range of these accounts is part of their force. Chris Edwards, of Tamil descent and raised in Prince George's County, Maryland, was deported in 2011, under Obama, and has built a life in Bengaluru, where he runs a streetwear label, makes music and is raising a daughter. Yasmany Moreno de Armas, a Cuban national detained for years in Florida, was shackled onto a plane he was told was bound for Cuba and learned mid-flight that it was heading to Africa. He reports that he has been held since July in a facility in the Central African Republic, allowed out for two hours a day, and he has gathered close to 40,000 followers on Instagram.

What makes these videos politically awkward is not their tone, which is often cheerful, but the gap they expose between public belief and policy. Hagenah cites a 2025 Pew Research Center survey in which nearly all respondents who favoured some deportations backed removing people with violent records, while support split sharply over those with nonviolent convictions or none at all. Many viewers, Tosh suggests, do not realise that deportees have frequently already served their sentences, and that the absence of research leaves immigration judges relying on thin evidence when weighing what removal will mean.

It would be easy to romanticise the deportee-influencer as a figure of resilience, and the article is wise not to. Edwards says he has yet to earn anything from his posts; Moreno de Armas depends on donations and on news channels that buy his footage. Visibility, moreover, is rationed by platforms whose algorithms decide whose story travels, and Hagenah recalls Human Rights Watch's 2023 finding that Meta suppressed Palestine-related content on Instagram. The same feeds, she notes, are filling with AI-generated anti-immigrant videos.

The deeper argument concerns knowledge and its politics. A state that tracks removals with precision but declines to follow their consequences has made a choice about what counts as its business, and the testimony of the expelled becomes, almost by default, the only archive. Hagenah ends by turning to her readers: whether they watch, pay, share or comment, they are now implicated in what these accounts reveal.

glossary.en: a book or record of accounts; here, figuratively, an official register of who belongs
to fill a gap left by the absence of information or action
to pass repeatedly in and out of an institution or condition
uncomfortable for those in power because it raises inconvenient questions
to divide clearly into opposing camps
evidence that is scant or weak
to present something as more appealing or heroic than it really is
to allow only a limited amount of something
because nothing else is available, not by choice
involved in, and bearing some responsibility for

items.grammar: Look at 'What makes these videos politically awkward is not their tone ... but the gap they expose'. This is a pseudo-cleft (wh-cleft): a 'what'-clause becomes the subject and the focused information is delayed until after 'is'. Combined with 'not X but Y', it lets the writer set up a question in the reader's mind and then correct the obvious answer. The first paragraph uses the same device: 'What happens next ... is simply not counted'.
items.grammar_zh: 注意 'What makes these videos politically awkward is not their tone ... but the gap they expose'。这是 what 引导的假拟分裂句：what 从句作主语，要强调的信息放在 is 之后。与 'not X but Y' 连用，作者先在读者心中提出问题，再纠正显而易见的答案。第一段的 'What happens next ... is simply not counted' 也用了同样的结构。
questions: Why does the article treat the absence of official data on deportees' lives as a political choice rather than an oversight?
In what ways do platform economics limit what deportee videos can achieve as testimony?
Hagenah casts viewers as implicated in what they watch. Is this a persuasive way to end, or does it shift responsibility away from the state?

sources.title: The Deportation Influencers (Iliana Hagenah, The Nation, 24 November 2026)

items.title: The Fighting Temeraire: a ghost ship at sunset
items.dek: A famous painting by Turner shows an old warship on her last journey, and a small, dark steam tug pulling her home.
paragraphs: Have you ever stood in front of a painting and felt sad and happy at the same time? Many visitors to the National Gallery in London have had that feeling in front of one glowing picture. It is called The Fighting Temeraire. The British artist J. M. W. Turner showed it in 1839. It is oil on canvas and about 1.2 metres wide, so it is smaller than most people expect.

The picture shows a real ship. HMS Temeraire was a huge wooden warship with 98 guns, and her wood came from more than 5,000 oak trees. In 1805 she fought at the Battle of Trafalgar and helped to defend Nelson's flagship, Victory. Her great days were soon over. From 1820 she was a supply ship, lying in the water near Sheerness, and in 1838 the navy sold her.

The buyer was John Beatson, who broke up old ships at Rotherhithe in London. He paid £5,530 for her. Two steam tugs pulled the old ship up the River Thames, and the journey took about two days. Turner has often been described as an artist of the sea, but he probably did not see this tow himself. He made the painting from reports of what happened.

Now look at the colours. The tall ship is pale and almost ghostly. The little tug is dark and busy, and it pushes out black smoke. Behind them the sky glows with orange, gold and red. Turner changed the facts to make a better picture. He gave the ship white and gold paint, and he put the tug's funnel in front of its mast, so the smoke blows back through the old ship's masts.

He also placed the setting sun in a way that does not fit the real journey. Artists call this "poetic licence": they are free to change a fact if the change helps the feeling. Many people have read the painting as a goodbye to the age of sailing ships and the arrival of the steam age. Turner never explained it in this way, so you can decide for yourself.

Later, someone made an engraving of the painting and "corrected" the funnel. Turner was furious. He kept the picture until he died in 1851, and he called it "his Darling". After his death it came to the nation, and it is now one of the most popular paintings in the National Gallery. Millions of people have already walked past it, and many have stopped to look for a long time.
paragraphs_zh: 你有没有站在一幅画前，同时感到悲伤又快乐？很多参观伦敦国家美术馆的人，在一幅发着光的画前都有过这种感觉。这幅画叫《战舰无畏号》（The Fighting Temeraire）。英国艺术家 J. M. W. 透纳于 1839 年展出了它。它是布面油画，约 1.2 米宽，比大多数人想象的要小。
画中是一艘真实的船。“无畏号”（HMS Temeraire）是一艘巨大的木制战舰，有 98 门炮，用了五千多棵橡树的木材。1805 年她参加了特拉法尔加海战，并帮助保护纳尔逊的旗舰“胜利号”。不久之后，她的辉煌岁月就结束了。从 1820 年起，她成了一艘补给船，停在希尔内斯附近的水面上，1838 年海军把她卖掉了。
买家是约翰·比特森，他在伦敦的罗瑟希德拆解旧船。他花了 5530 英镑买下这艘船。两艘蒸汽拖船把这艘老船沿泰晤士河拖上去，航程大约两天。人们常说透纳是画海的艺术家，但他很可能没有亲眼看到这次拖行。他是根据报道把画画出来的。
现在来看颜色。高大的船苍白，几乎像幽灵。小拖船黑黑的，忙碌地冒着黑烟。它们身后的天空闪耀着橙色、金色和红色。透纳改动了事实，让画面更动人。他给这艘船涂上了白色和金色，还把拖船的烟囱画在桅杆前面，所以烟向后吹过老船的桅杆。
他还把落日放在一个与真实航程不符的位置。艺术家把这叫作“诗意的自由”：只要改动能帮助表达感情，他们就可以改变事实。很多人把这幅画解读为对帆船时代的告别，以及蒸汽时代的到来。透纳从没有这样解释过，所以你可以自己决定。
后来有人为这幅画制作了版画，并“更正”了烟囱的位置。透纳非常愤怒。他一直保留这幅画到 1851 年去世，并称它为“他的宝贝”。他去世后，这幅画归了国家，现在是国家美术馆最受欢迎的画作之一。数百万人已经从它面前走过，很多人还停下来看了很久。

glossary.en: a large ship built for war
a ship that carries food and other things for other ships
a small strong boat that pulls bigger ships
the tall pipe on a ship where smoke goes out
pale and strange, like a ghost
to shine with a soft, warm light
to take a ship apart, usually to sell the parts
the freedom of an artist to change facts for a better effect
glossary.zh: 艺术加工的自由；诗意的自由

items.grammar: We use the present perfect (have/has + past participle) to talk about experience and results, without saying exactly when. Look at "Have you ever stood in front of a painting…?" and "Millions of people have already walked past it." Ever is for questions, never is for "not at any time", just means a very short time ago, and already means earlier than expected. When we say exactly when ("in 1839", "in 1805"), we use the past simple: "Turner showed it in 1839."
items.grammar_zh: 现在完成时（have/has + 过去分词）用来谈经历和结果，不说明具体时间。例如文中的 “Have you ever stood in front of a painting…?” 和 “Millions of people have already walked past it.” ever 用于问句，意思是“曾经”；never 表示“从未”；just 表示“刚刚”；already 表示“已经（比预期早）”。一旦说出具体时间（in 1839、in 1805），就要用一般过去时：“Turner showed it in 1839.” 汉语常用“过”“了”“已经”表达类似意思，但英语必须用 have/has + 过去分词这一形式。
questions: Why do you think Turner made the ship pale and the tug dark?
Which do you find more interesting in a painting: the real facts or the artist's feelings?
And you? Have you ever seen a painting that made you feel something strong? What was it?

sources.title: The Fighting Temeraire (NG524), National Gallery, London

items.title: En una casa de cambio en Cali: quisiera cambiar euros
items.dek: Clara, una turista, cambia dinero en Cali, pregunta por un cajero automático y pide una recomendación para almorzar.
paragraphs: Daniela: Buenas tardes. ¿En qué le puedo ayudar?
Clara: Buenas tardes. Quisiera cambiar cien euros a pesos, por favor.
Daniela: Claro que sí. ¿Me permite su pasaporte? Lo necesito para el registro.
Clara: Sí, aquí lo tiene. ¿Cuánto me dan por cada euro?
Daniela: La tasa de hoy está en la pantalla, a su derecha. Se la puedo imprimir si quiere.
Clara: No hace falta, gracias. ¿Cobran comisión?
Daniela: No, aquí no cobramos comisión. Le damos el valor completo.
Clara: Perfecto. Entonces quisiera cambiar los cien. Y quisiera preguntar algo más: ¿dónde queda un cajero automático?
Daniela: Hay uno en la esquina, al lado de la farmacia. Salga y siga derecho una cuadra.
Clara: ¿Y después doblo a la izquierda?
Daniela: No, no tiene que doblar. Queda justo en esa esquina, al frente del parque.
Clara: Muchas gracias. Y una última pregunta: ¿me recomienda un lugar para almorzar cerca de aquí?
Daniela: Con gusto. A dos cuadras hay un restaurante con muy buen sancocho y jugo de lulo.
Clara: ¡Qué rico! Gracias por todo, Daniela.
Daniela: Con mucho gusto. ¡Que le vaya bien en Cali!
Dato curioso: Cali es famosa por la salsa, y por eso mucha gente la llama la «capital mundial de la salsa».
paragraphs_en: Daniela: Good afternoon. How can I help you?
Clara: Good afternoon. I would like to change one hundred euros into pesos, please.
Daniela: Of course. May I have your passport? I need it for the record.
Clara: Yes, here you are. How much do I get for each euro?
Daniela: Today's rate is on the screen, to your right. I can print it for you if you like.
Clara: That's not necessary, thanks. Do you charge a commission?
Daniela: No, we don't charge a commission here. We give you the full value.
Clara: Perfect. Then I would like to change all hundred. And I would like to ask something else: where is an ATM?
Daniela: There is one on the corner, next to the pharmacy. Go out and keep straight for one block.
Clara: And then I turn left?
Daniela: No, you don't have to turn. It is right on that corner, across from the park.
Clara: Thank you very much. And one last question: can you recommend a place to have lunch near here?
Daniela: With pleasure. Two blocks away there is a restaurant with very good sancocho (soup) and lulo juice.
Clara: How delicious! Thanks for everything, Daniela.
Daniela: You're welcome. Have a good time in Cali!
Fun fact: Cali is famous for salsa, and many people call it the "world capital of salsa."
paragraphs_de: Daniela: Guten Tag. Wie kann ich Ihnen helfen?
Clara: Guten Tag. Ich möchte bitte hundert Euro in Pesos wechseln.
Daniela: Gern. Darf ich Ihren Reisepass sehen? Ich brauche ihn für die Registrierung.
Clara: Ja, hier bitte. Wie viel bekomme ich für jeden Euro?
Daniela: Der heutige Kurs steht auf dem Bildschirm, rechts von Ihnen. Ich kann ihn Ihnen ausdrucken, wenn Sie möchten.
Clara: Das ist nicht nötig, danke. Nehmen Sie eine Gebühr?
Daniela: Nein, wir nehmen hier keine Gebühr. Sie bekommen den vollen Wert.
Clara: Perfekt. Dann möchte ich alle hundert wechseln. Und ich möchte noch etwas fragen: Wo ist ein Geldautomat?
Daniela: Einer ist an der Ecke, neben der Apotheke. Gehen Sie hinaus und dann einen Block geradeaus.
Clara: Und danach biege ich links ab?
Daniela: Nein, Sie müssen nicht abbiegen. Er ist genau an dieser Ecke, gegenüber vom Park.
Clara: Vielen Dank. Und eine letzte Frage: Können Sie mir ein Lokal zum Mittagessen in der Nähe empfehlen?
Daniela: Gern. Zwei Blocks weiter gibt es ein Restaurant mit sehr gutem Sancocho (Suppe) und Lulo-Saft.
Clara: Wie lecker! Danke für alles, Daniela.
Daniela: Gern geschehen. Gute Zeit in Cali!
Wissenswertes: Cali ist berühmt für Salsa, deshalb nennen viele Leute die Stadt die „Salsa-Hauptstadt der Welt“.
items.grammar: For polite requests, use quisiera + infinitive: “Quisiera cambiar cien euros.” It sounds softer than quiero and is perfect for shops, banks and hotels. You can also use it to ask a question politely: “Quisiera preguntar algo.” The employee uses usted (“¿Me permite su pasaporte?”), so the same polite tone works both ways.
items.grammar_de: Für höfliche Bitten benutzt man quisiera + Infinitiv: „Quisiera cambiar cien euros.“ Das klingt weicher als quiero und passt gut in Geschäfte, Banken und Hotels. Man kann es auch für eine höfliche Frage nutzen: „Quisiera preguntar algo.“ Die Angestellte sagt usted („¿Me permite su pasaporte?“), also gilt derselbe höfliche Ton in beide Richtungen.
questions: ¿Qué quisieras comprar o hacer en Cali?
¿Y tú? ¿Cómo prefieres pagar cuando viajas: con efectivo o con tarjeta?
En la conversación, ¿qué dos indicaciones da Daniela para llegar al cajero?

items.title: Guaraní: el idioma que Paraguay habla en voz alta
items.dek: En Paraguay, dos idiomas oficiales conviven en la calle, en la escuela y en la misma frase.
paragraphs: Si caminas por Asunción un día cualquiera, es probable que oigas dos idiomas en la misma conversación, y a veces en la misma frase. Paraguay es uno de los pocos países de América donde una lengua indígena no solo sobrevive, sino que la habla gran parte de la población. Desde la Constitución de 1992, el guaraní y el español son los dos idiomas oficiales del país. Es decir, una persona puede hablar con un juez, ir al médico o estudiar en la escuela usando cualquiera de los dos, y eso cambia la vida diaria de mucha gente.

Esta situación no siempre fue tan favorable para el guaraní. Durante mucho tiempo se dijo que era una lengua «de la casa» y que el español era la lengua del progreso. Por eso, muchas familias decidieron hablar solo español con sus hijos, con la esperanza de que tuvieran más oportunidades. Con los años, sin embargo, cambió la actitud: la reforma educativa de los años noventa introdujo la educación bilingüe, y una ley de 2010 creó la Secretaría de Políticas Lingüísticas para proteger y promover los idiomas del país.

En la calle, lo que más se oye es el jopara, una mezcla natural de guaraní y español. Una persona puede empezar una frase en español, seguir en guaraní y terminar con una palabra de cada idioma, sin pensarlo ni un segundo. Muchos lingüistas explican que esto no es un error, sino una forma real de hablar que refleja siglos de convivencia entre las dos lenguas. Quienes defienden el guaraní, en cambio, recuerdan que también existe un guaraní más formal, el que se enseña en las escuelas y se usa en los libros.

Si quieres practicar un poco, aprende dos expresiones. Para saludar se dice «Mba'éichapa», que significa más o menos «¿cómo estás?», y para dar las gracias se dice «aguyje». Las personas que viajan a Paraguay cuentan que, cuando alguien dice unas pocas palabras en guaraní, la conversación se vuelve más cálida enseguida. No hace falta hablar perfectamente: el esfuerzo se agradece. Además, aprender unas frases te ayuda a entender mejor cómo piensan y cómo se sienten las personas que las usan todos los días.

El guaraní tampoco se queda dentro de las fronteras de Paraguay. También se habla en regiones de Argentina, Bolivia y Brasil, y el español de toda la zona usa palabras que vienen de esta lengua. Además, cada 25 de agosto se celebra el Día del Idioma Guaraní, una fecha en la que se organizan actividades en escuelas y comunidades. Para mucha gente, el idioma es una parte importante de la identidad del país, y también de su futuro.
Dato curioso: el español que hablas también tiene palabras guaraníes. Ñandú, el ave grande que no vuela, y yacaré, un reptil parecido al cocodrilo, vienen del guaraní.
paragraphs_en: If you walk around Asunción on any ordinary day, you will probably hear two languages in the same conversation, and sometimes in the same sentence. Paraguay is one of the few countries in the Americas where an indigenous language not only survives but is spoken by a large part of the population. Since the 1992 Constitution, Guaraní and Spanish have been the country's two official languages. In other words, a person can speak with a judge, see a doctor or study at school using either of them, and that changes the daily life of many people.

This situation was not always so favorable for Guaraní. For a long time people said that it was a language “of the home” and that Spanish was the language of progress. For that reason, many families decided to speak only Spanish with their children, hoping they would have more opportunities. Over the years, however, attitudes changed: the education reform of the 1990s introduced bilingual education, and a law from 2010 created the Secretariat of Language Policies to protect and promote the country's languages.

On the street, what you hear most is jopara, a natural mix of Guaraní and Spanish. A person can start a sentence in Spanish, continue in Guaraní and finish with one word from each language, without thinking about it for a second. Many linguists explain that this is not a mistake but a real way of speaking that reflects centuries of coexistence between the two languages. Those who defend Guaraní, on the other hand, remind us that there is also a more formal Guaraní, the one taught in schools and used in books.

If you want to practice a little, learn two expressions. To greet someone you say “Mba'éichapa,” which means roughly “how are you?”, and to say thank you you say “aguyje.” People who travel to Paraguay say that when someone speaks just a few words of Guaraní, the conversation becomes warmer right away. You don't have to speak perfectly: the effort is appreciated. Besides, learning a few phrases helps you understand better how the people who use them every day think and feel.

Guaraní doesn't stay inside Paraguay's borders either. It is also spoken in regions of Argentina, Bolivia and Brazil, and the Spanish of the whole area uses words that come from this language. In addition, every August 25 the Day of the Guaraní Language is celebrated, a date on which activities are organized in schools and communities. For many people, the language is an important part of the country's identity, and also of its future.
Fun fact: the Spanish you speak also has Guaraní words. Ñandú, the large flightless bird (rhea), and yacaré, a reptile similar to a crocodile (caiman), come from Guaraní.
paragraphs_de: Wenn du an einem beliebigen Tag durch Asunción gehst, hörst du wahrscheinlich zwei Sprachen im selben Gespräch, manchmal sogar im selben Satz. Paraguay ist eines der wenigen Länder Amerikas, in denen eine indigene Sprache nicht nur überlebt, sondern von einem großen Teil der Bevölkerung gesprochen wird. Seit der Verfassung von 1992 sind Guaraní und Spanisch die beiden Amtssprachen des Landes. Das heißt, eine Person kann mit einem Richter sprechen, zum Arzt gehen oder in der Schule lernen und dabei eine der beiden Sprachen benutzen, und das verändert den Alltag vieler Menschen.

Diese Lage war für das Guaraní nicht immer so günstig. Lange Zeit sagte man, es sei eine Sprache „für zu Hause“, und Spanisch sei die Sprache des Fortschritts. Deshalb entschieden sich viele Familien, mit ihren Kindern nur Spanisch zu sprechen, in der Hoffnung auf bessere Chancen. Mit den Jahren änderte sich die Haltung jedoch: Die Bildungsreform der 1990er Jahre führte zweisprachigen Unterricht ein, und ein Gesetz von 2010 schuf das Sekretariat für Sprachpolitik, um die Sprachen des Landes zu schützen und zu fördern.

Auf der Straße hört man am häufigsten Jopara, eine natürliche Mischung aus Guaraní und Spanisch. Eine Person kann einen Satz auf Spanisch beginnen, auf Guaraní weitersprechen und mit je einem Wort aus beiden Sprachen enden, ohne eine Sekunde darüber nachzudenken. Viele Sprachwissenschaftler erklären, dass das kein Fehler ist, sondern eine echte Sprechweise, die Jahrhunderte des Zusammenlebens beider Sprachen widerspiegelt. Wer das Guaraní verteidigt, erinnert dagegen daran, dass es auch ein formelleres Guaraní gibt, das in der Schule gelehrt und in Büchern verwendet wird.

Wenn du ein wenig üben möchtest, lerne zwei Ausdrücke. Zum Begrüßen sagt man „Mba'éichapa“, das ungefähr „Wie geht's?“ bedeutet, und zum Danken sagt man „aguyje“. Wer nach Paraguay reist, erzählt, dass das Gespräch sofort wärmer wird, wenn jemand ein paar Wörter Guaraní spricht. Man muss nicht perfekt sprechen: Die Mühe wird geschätzt. Außerdem hilft dir das Lernen einiger Sätze, besser zu verstehen, wie die Menschen denken und fühlen, die sie jeden Tag benutzen.

Das Guaraní bleibt auch nicht innerhalb der Grenzen Paraguays. Es wird auch in Regionen von Argentinien, Bolivien und Brasilien gesprochen, und das Spanisch der ganzen Gegend benutzt Wörter, die aus dieser Sprache stammen. Außerdem wird jedes Jahr am 25. August der Tag der Guaraní-Sprache gefeiert, an dem in Schulen und Gemeinden Aktivitäten stattfinden. Für viele Menschen ist die Sprache ein wichtiger Teil der Identität des Landes und auch seiner Zukunft.
Wissenswertes: Auch das Spanisch, das du sprichst, hat Wörter aus dem Guaraní. Ñandú, der große flugunfähige Vogel (Nandu), und yacaré, ein krokodilähnliches Reptil (Kaiman), stammen aus dem Guaraní.

glossary.en: to defend, to stand up for
to appreciate, to be thankful for

items.grammar: Reported speech (B2) tells what someone said or what people say, without quoting. After a verb like decir, explicar or contar, use que. If the main verb is in the past, the verb inside the “que” clause usually moves back too: “Se dijo que era una lengua de la casa” (the original idea: “es una lengua de la casa”). If the main verb is in the present, the tense stays: “Muchos lingüistas explican que esto no es un error.” Keep the same logic with pronouns and time words.
items.grammar_de: Die indirekte Rede (B2) gibt wieder, was jemand gesagt hat oder was Leute sagen, ohne zu zitieren. Nach Verben wie decir, explicar oder contar steht que. Steht das Hauptverb in der Vergangenheit, rutscht meist auch das Verb im que-Satz zurück: „Se dijo que era una lengua de la casa“ (ursprünglich: „es una lengua de la casa“). Steht das Hauptverb im Präsens, bleibt die Zeit gleich: „Muchos lingüistas explican que esto no es un error.“ Dieselbe Logik gilt für Pronomen und Zeitwörter.
questions: ¿Por qué muchas familias dejaron de hablar guaraní con sus hijos durante un tiempo?
¿Qué es el jopara y por qué muchos lingüistas dicen que no es un error?
¿Y tú? ¿Hablas o conoces alguna lengua que se mezcla con otra en tu región o en tu familia?

items.title: Bilhete na geladeira: a chave, a ração e o Tito
items.dek: No sábado, a Ana passa o dia fora e a Dona Rosa cuida do Tito. Na porta da geladeira tem um bilhete — com um P.S. muito importante.
paragraphs: Querida Dona Rosa,
Obrigada! A minha chave está debaixo do vaso de flores.
A ração do Tito está no armário da cozinha. A tigela dele é a azul.
Ele come às oito e às seis. Só um pouco!
O brinquedo dele: a bola vermelha, no sofá.
P.S.: O Tito diz: “A cama do Bolinha é minha.” Não é!
Beijos, Ana
paragraphs_en: Dear Dona Rosa,
Thank you! My key is under the flower pot.
Tito's food is in the kitchen cupboard. His bowl is the blue one.
He eats at eight and at six. Just a little!
His toy is the red ball, on the sofa.
P.S.: Tito says: “Bolinha's bed is mine.” It isn't!
Kisses, Ana
paragraphs_zh: 谢谢您！我的钥匙在花盆下面。
蒂托的猫粮在厨房的柜子里。它的碗是蓝色的那个。
它八点和六点吃饭。只吃一点点！
它的玩具是那个红球，在沙发上。
附言：蒂托说：“小球的床是我的。”才不是！
paragraphs_de: Liebe Dona Rosa,
Danke! Mein Schlüssel liegt unter dem Blumentopf.
Titos Futter ist im Küchenschrank. Sein Napf ist der blaue.
Er frisst um acht und um sechs. Nur ein bisschen!
Sein Spielzeug ist der rote Ball, auf dem Sofa.
PS: Tito sagt: „Bolinhas Bett gehört mir.“ Stimmt nicht!
Küsschen, Ana

glossary.pt: Uma mensagem curta no papel. O bilhete está na geladeira.
Com a chave, a gente abre a porta.
Embaixo, o contrário de em cima. Debaixo do vaso = embaixo do vaso.
Uma coisa com terra e flores dentro.
Um móvel com portas. No armário da cozinha tem pratos e comida.
Uma coisa para brincar. A bola é um brinquedo.
Não muito. Só um pouco de ração.

items.grammar: Before a noun, the possessive usually comes with the article: a minha chave (my key), a tigela dele (his bowl). After ser, it often stands alone, without the article: A cama é minha. (The bed is mine.) — A chave é sua? (Is the key yours?)
items.grammar_zh: 放在名词前时，物主代词通常带冠词：a minha chave（我的钥匙），a tigela dele（它的碗）。在 ser 后面，常常单独使用、不带冠词：A cama é minha.（床是我的。）— A chave é sua?（钥匙是你的吗？）
items.grammar_de: Vor einem Nomen steht das Possessiv meist mit Artikel: a minha chave (mein Schlüssel), a tigela dele (sein Napf). Nach ser steht es oft allein, ohne Artikel: A cama é minha. (Das Bett gehört mir.) — A chave é sua? (Ist das dein Schlüssel?)
items.grammar_pt: Antes da palavra, a gente usa o artigo: a minha chave, a tigela dele. Depois de ser, muitas vezes sem artigo: A cama é minha. A chave é sua?
questions: Onde está a chave da Ana?
Qual é a tigela do Tito? E o brinquedo dele?
E você? Onde está a sua chave agora?
